derivations.claim:
For an integer $M\ge2$, integration by parts in $\mathbf x$ gives
$$(1+|\mathbf k|^2)^M\widehat\phi_t(\mathbf k)=\widehat{(1-\Delta_{\mathbf x})^M\phi(t,\cdot)}(\mathbf k).$$
Every boundary term vanishes because $\phi$ is Schwartz. For any fixed $L>3$, Schwartz seminorms bound
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}|(1-\Delta_{\mathbf x})^M\phi(t,\mathbf x)|\,d^3\mathbf x\le C_M(\phi)(1+|t|)^{-2}\int_{\mathbb R^3}(1+|\mathbf x|)^{-L}d^3\mathbf x,$$
so $|\widehat\phi_t(-\mathbf k)|\le C'_M(\phi)(1+|t|)^{-2}(1+|\mathbf k|^2)^{-M}$. The $t$ bound is integrable. In radial $\mathbf k$ coordinates the shell weight is at most a constant times $r\,dr$ because $\omega_\mu(r)\ge r$; hence its product with $(1+r^2)^{-M}$ is integrable at infinity and at $r=0$, including $\mu=0$. Thus the defining integral converges absolutely and is bounded by a finite Schwartz seminorm, proving that $H_\mu$ is tempered.

For each $\omega>0$, let $g_\omega(t)=e^{-i\omega|t|}/(2\omega)$. It is continuous at $0$, with $g_\omega'(0+)=-i/2$ and $g_\omega'(0-)=+i/2$. For a compactly supported smooth test $\eta(t)$, integrating by parts separately on $(-\infty,0)$ and $(0,\infty)$ cancels the boundary terms involving $\eta'(0)$ and leaves the derivative jump times $\eta(0)$; since $g_\omega''=-\omega^2g_\omega$ off $0$, this proves
$$g_\omega''+\omega^2g_\omega=-i\delta_0$$
as a one-dimensional distribution.

By [F4, F5] and Fubini's theorem [F7], the positive-frequency two-point kernel is
$$W_\mu(t,\mathbf x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)}e^{-i\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)t+i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}$$
as a distribution. This is the slice of $H_\mu$ for $t>0$. For $t<0$, replacing $\mathbf k$ by $-\mathbf k$ identifies its slice with $W_\mu(-t,-\mathbf x);$ the same substitution proves $H_\mu(t,\mathbf x)=H_\mu(-t,-\mathbf x)$. For real tests, the vacuum expectation of the field commutator is $W_\mu(f,g)-W_\mu(g,f)$; [F6] identifies it with a distribution supported in the causal cone. Thus the two Wightman orderings agree on spacelike-separated supports. For a compactly supported smooth spatial test supported away from $\mathbf x=0$, both slice pairings are continuous in $t$ by [F9] and the integrable bound in 1.1, so no additional term supported at $t=0$ occurs away from the coincidence point. The partial Fourier formula itself specifies the extension at coincidence.

The spatial Fourier multiplier of $\Box-\mu^2$ is $-\partial_t^2-|\mathbf k|^2-\mu^2=-(\partial_t^2+\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)^2)$. Applying it to the kernel in 2.1 and using 1.2 gives $i\delta_0(t)$ times $(2\pi)^{-3}\int e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}d^3\mathbf k$. Fourier inversion [F8] identifies the latter as $\delta_0(\mathbf x)$. For $\mu=0$ the excluded apex has measure zero and the shell weight is locally integrable there, as established in 1.1; it contributes no additional distribution. Therefore $(\Box-\mu^2)H_\mu=i\delta_0$ in four dimensions.

For the scalar action, differentiating its density at $\phi+\varepsilon h$ gives
$$\delta S_\phi=-\int_{\mathbb R^4}\left(\eta^{ab}\partial_a\phi\,\partial_b h+\mu^2\phi h\right)d^4x.$$
For each coordinate, the product $\partial_a\phi\,h$ has compact support; one-dimensional integration by parts on that coordinate has zero boundary term, and Fubini [F4] permits integrating the remaining coordinates. Hence
$$\delta S_\phi=\int_{\mathbb R^4}h\left(\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b\phi-\mu^2\phi\right)d^4x=\int_{\mathbb R^4}h(\Box-\mu^2)\phi\,d^4x.$$

Put $R_D=(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi$. From [F1], $\beta^\dagger=\beta$ and $\beta^2=I_4$. Each $\sigma_j$ is Hermitian, so $\alpha_j^\dagger=\alpha_j$; the off-diagonal blocks give $\alpha_j\beta=-\beta\alpha_j$. Hence $\gamma^0=\beta$ is Hermitian and $(\gamma^j)^\dagger=(\beta\alpha_j)^\dagger=\alpha_j\beta=-\beta\alpha_j=-\gamma^j$, so $(\gamma^a)^\dagger\beta=\beta\gamma^a$ for every $a$. Varying $\psi$ and $\bar\psi=\psi^\dagger\beta$ together along a real parameter gives
$$\delta S_D=\int_{\mathbb R^4}\bar\chi R_D+\bar\psi(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\chi\,d^4x.$$
Integrating the second term by parts coordinatewise, with zero boundary terms since $\chi$ is compactly supported, yields
$$\delta S_D=\int_{\mathbb R^4}\bar\chi R_D+\left(-i\partial_a\bar\psi\,\gamma^a-\mu\bar\psi\right)\chi\,d^4x=2\operatorname{Re}\int_{\mathbb R^4}\chi^\dagger\beta R_D\,d^4x,$$
because $R_D^\dagger\beta=-i\partial_a\bar\psi\,\gamma^a-\mu\bar\psi$.

If $(\Box-\mu^2)\phi=0$, step 1.1 makes every variation vanish. Conversely, if the smooth residual $R_\phi=(\Box-\mu^2)\phi$ is nonzero at a point, continuity gives a ball on which it has one strict sign; choosing the nonnegative bump from [F3] inside that ball gives $\int hR_\phi\ne0$. Thus scalar stationarity for all compactly supported real $h$ is equivalent to the Klein–Gordon equation.

If $R_D=0$, step 1.2 gives stationarity. Conversely, if $R_D(x_0)\ne0$, continuity gives a ball on which $|R_D|>0$. Choose a nonnegative bump $\rho$ supported there and positive on a smaller ball [F3], and take the admissible variation $\chi=\rho\,\beta R_D$. Then
$$\delta S_D=2\int_{\mathbb R^4}\rho\,|R_D|^2\,d^4x>0,$$
contradicting stationarity. Thus $R_D=0$ pointwise. Its adjoint is $-i\partial_a\bar\psi\,\gamma^a-\mu\bar\psi=0$, and conversely that adjoint equation implies $R_D=0$ since $\beta$ is invertible.
